title: A/B testing basics
examples: How do I know if the difference I see is real?
What is the minimum number of users I need to test this on?
What exactly is the control group in this context?

explain.say: Today we are learning about A/B testing basics. This helps us compare two versions to see which performs better.
The first concept is the control group. This group sees the original version, or the baseline experience.
Next we look at sample size. This is the total number of users you need to test on for reliable results.
Then we discuss statistical significance. This tells us if the difference is real or just random chance.

draw.text: Significance: Is it Real or Luck?

explain.say: For example, if you change a button color, the control group sees blue, and the variation sees green.
In real life, a streaming service might test two different recommendation layouts. One group sees the old layout, and the other sees the new one.

faq.q: What is the difference between statistical significance and correlation?
faq.a: Correlation means two things move together, but significance means the relationship is unlikely due to chance. You can correlate things without them being truly related.

faq.q: If my sample size is too small, what happens to my results?
faq.a: Small samples mean your results are highly susceptible to random variation. A few unusual users can skew your entire conclusion.
asks: Can I just run the test for longer?
What is the risk of small sample size?

faq.q: Should I always use a control group?
faq.a: Yes, using a control group is best practice. It provides a direct baseline against which to measure any change.
asks: What if I don't have an original version?

faq.q: How do I calculate the necessary sample size?
faq.a: This usually requires knowing your baseline conversion rate and the minimum detectable effect you hope to find. Specialized calculators are best for this.
asks: Is there a formula for sample size?
What inputs do I need for sample size?

faq.q: What is a minimum detectable effect?
faq.a: It is the smallest improvement or decrease you want your test to be powerful enough to actually detect. You must define this before testing.
asks: Why do I need to set this beforehand?
What if I don't know this value?

facts: A/B testing compares two versions: a control and a variation.
The control group always sees the existing, unchanged version.
Sample size must be large enough to detect a meaningful difference.
Statistical significance helps rule out random chance as the cause.

quiz.say: A website redesign changes the checkout button from red to blue. The control group sees red, and the variation sees blue. If the blue button shows a 5% lift, what is the first thing to check?

options.show: The sample size must be sufficient to support the observed lift.
options.say: The sample size must be sufficient to support the observed lift.

options.show: The blue button is definitely better; implement it now.
options.say: The blue button is definitely better; implement it now.

options.show: The lift is only significant if it is over 10%.
options.say: The lift is only significant if it is over 10%.

options.show: I should just test it on a different day.
options.say: I should just test it on a different day.

quiz.why: A large sample size ensures the 5% lift is likely real and not just a fluke of a few users.

wrong.1: This ignores the possibility that the initial test group was unusually lucky.
wrong.2: Significance is based on probability, not a fixed percentage threshold.
wrong.3: Testing on different days introduces external variables that confuse the results.

quiz.say: A marketing team tests two email subject lines. The control uses 'Sale Today!' and the variation uses 'Limited Time Offer.' The variation performs better. What is the next crucial step?

options.show: Determine if the difference is statistically significant.
options.say: Determine if the difference is statistically significant.

options.show: Immediately send the new subject line to everyone.
options.say: Immediately send the new subject line to everyone.

options.show: Increase the sample size by half and retest.
options.say: Increase the sample size by half and retest.

options.show: Just pick the subject line that sounds better to the marketing manager.
options.say: Just pick the subject line that sounds better to the marketing manager.

quiz.why: You must confirm that the observed improvement is reliable and not due to random chance.

wrong.1: You might be acting on a result that is only coincidental.
wrong.2: You should first check the existing sample size calculation before increasing it arbitrarily.
wrong.3: Subjectivity is not a valid measure for optimizing user behavior.

quiz.say: A checkout page is tested. Control: 1000 users, 10% conversion. Variation: 1000 users, 12% conversion. Which statement is the most responsible conclusion?

options.show: The result suggests improvement, but further testing is needed for confidence.
options.say: The result suggests improvement, but further testing is needed for confidence.

options.show: The new design is definitely better; implement it now.
options.say: The new design is definitely better; implement it now.

options.show: The difference is too small to bother implementing.
options.say: The difference is too small to bother implementing.

options.show: We must wait until we reach 10,000 users to decide anything.
options.say: We must wait until we reach 10,000 users to decide anything.

quiz.why: A 2% lift is promising, but without knowing the required sample size, you cannot make a final decision.

wrong.1: This overstates the certainty of the result without confirming statistical significance.
wrong.2: Even small, significant improvements can lead to large revenue gains over time.
wrong.3: While more data is good, waiting indefinitely prevents optimization.
